title: The Incarnation: the Word Became Flesh
lead: The Christian belief that the eternal Son of God became a real human being, Jesus of Nazareth, without ceasing to be God: 'And the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us' (John 1:14). The New Testament states it in hymns and confessions; Ignatius of Antioch, early in the second century, defended it against teachers who said Christ only seemed to be human; the councils of Nicaea and Chalcedon put it into the words of the creeds. Judaism does not hold it. (The denial that Christ had a real body has its own page, Docetism; the manner of Jesus' conception is The Virgin Birth.)

sections.h: God with us: the Old Testament frame
sections.b: Matthew reads the birth of Jesus as the sign of Isaiah: 'Look, the virgin will be pregnant and will have a son, and they will give him the name Immanuel' (Matthew 1:23), adding that the name means 'God is with us'. In Isaiah, where the site translates from the Hebrew, the sign reads 'Look, the young woman is pregnant and about to have a son, and she will name him Immanuel' (Isaiah 7:14); the notes there take up the word. Behind John's 'pitched his tent' stands God's promise for the tabernacle: 'They are to make me a holy place, and I will live in their midst' (Exodus 25:8). Revelation ends with the same picture in Greek tent words (skēnē, skēnoō): 'Look! God's tent is with human beings. He will pitch his tent with them' (Revelation 21:3).

John's Gospel opens with the Word who 'was with God, and ... was God' (John 1:1), and then says the thing no one expected: 'And the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us. We gazed at his glory' (John 1:14). The Greek sarx, 'flesh', is the plain word for a human body and human weakness. 1 John begins the same way: 'what we have seen with our eyes, what we gazed at and our hands touched: this is what we speak of, the word of life' (1 John 1:1).

Paul writes that Christ, 'Being in the form of God', 'emptied himself, / taking a slave's form, / coming to be in the likeness of human beings' (Philippians 2:6-7); whether these lines are an older hymn that Paul quotes is taken up on the page Kenosis. 'God sent out his Son. He was born of a woman. He was born under the law' (Galatians 4:4). 'In him all the fullness of deity makes its home bodily' (Colossians 2:9). 1 Timothy, one of the Pastoral Letters, whose authorship is debated (see that book's page), sets out the same faith in lines that read like a confession: 'He was made visible in the flesh, / proven right in the Spirit' (1 Timothy 3:16).
sections.refs: Philippians 2:6-11; 1 Timothy 3:16; Galatians 4:4; Colossians 2:9; Romans 1:3-4; Romans 8:3

sections.b: Hebrews gives reasons. 'Since, then, the children have blood and flesh in common, he too took a share in these very things', so that by his death he could break the devil's power (Hebrews 2:14). 'This is why he was bound to become like his brothers in everything: to be a high priest who is merciful and faithful' (Hebrews 2:17). He has been 'tested in all things, in the same way we are, but apart from sin' (Hebrews 4:15).

sections.h: Come in the flesh: the first test
sections.b: Already in the New Testament the confession that Christ came 'in the flesh' marks the true faith: 'any spirit that confesses Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh is from God' (1 John 4:2), and those who 'do not confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh' are called deceivers (2 John 7). The risen Jesus himself insists on his body: 'a spirit has no flesh and bones, and you can see that I have them' (Luke 24:39).

Early in the second century Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to die in Rome, wrote to the church at Ephesus against teachers who said Christ only seemed to suffer. His answer is a chain of pairs: 'There is one doctor, / both of flesh and of spirit, / born and unborn, / God in man' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2). He calls Jesus 'our God' who 'was carried in the womb by Mary' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2), and says that at his coming 'God was made known in a human way' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:3). Two centuries later Athanasius quoted the line in the arguments over Arius, with 'God in man' but with 'born and unborn' spelled as 'originate and unoriginate' (Greek genētos kai agenētos), a difference the note at Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2 explains (On the Councils 47). Ignatius's letters are not Scripture for any church, but they show how the New Testament's teaching was held and defended in the next generation.
sections.refs: Ignatius to the Ephesians 7:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 18:2; Ignatius to the Ephesians 19:3; Ignatius to the Ephesians 20:2

sections.b: The Council of Nicaea (325) confessed one Lord Jesus Christ, 'very God of very God', who 'for us men and for our salvation came down [from heaven] and was incarnate and was made man'. The Council of Chalcedon (451) defined him as 'perfect in Godhead and perfect in manhood, very God and very man', one person 'in two natures, unconfusedly, immutably, indivisibly, inseparably [united]'. (Both are quoted from the English of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers.)

Judaism. In a Christian-Jewish dialogue published in 2008, Edward Kessler, writing the Jewish side, says that the incarnation 'is generally viewed as one of the main dividing lines between Judaism and Christianity', and that Jews 'reject the tremendous claim' made for Jesus, that he is 'God Incarnate': 'no person ... can possess the perfection of God'. He reports the Orthodox Jewish scholar Michael Wyschogrod as holding that for a Jew to accept the belief 'would mean a grave violation of the prohibition against idolatry', yet that Jews should not dismiss it out of hand, since to reject it on a priori grounds 'would be to impose external constraints on God's freedom'. Wyschogrod could even call Judaism 'incarnational', in the sense that God enters the human world and dwells among Israel, as the dialogue's Christian writer, Hans Hermann Henrix, quotes him.
